The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the **RMS Titanic**.

To understand the complex concepts of blockchain technology described in your text, we can use the analogy of a **shared, public notebook** kept by a large community.

Imagine a village where everyone wants to keep track of who owes whom money. Instead of trusting one person (like a bank or a single accountant) to hold the only copy of the ledger, every single villager gets their own identical notebook.

1.  **Decentralization (Copied across a thousand computers):**
    In this village, instead of one central book, every person has a copy. If one person’s notebook is lost or damaged, the others still have the record. This means no single point of failure exists. In blockchain terms, the "thousand different computers" are the nodes in the network, each holding a full copy of the transaction history.

2.  **Immutability and Verification (Changes must be verified and agreed upon):**
    Suppose Alice wants to record that she paid Bob $10. She doesn’t just write it in her own notebook and call it done. She shouts the transaction to the whole village. The other villagers check their own notebooks to see if Alice actually has $10. If they agree she does, they all write down the transaction in their own notebooks at the same time.
    
    Because everyone has the same copy, if a dishonest person tries to sneak into their house and erase "Alice paid Bob" from their notebook, it won’t matter. The other 999 villagers will look at their own notebooks, see the discrepancy, and reject the change. The majority must agree on the truth, making it extremely difficult for anyone to alter history without being detected.

3.  **Security and Trustworthiness:**
    This system is secure not because of a strong lock on a door, but because of the sheer number of people watching and verifying. You don’t need to trust a single bank manager; you trust the mathematical and social consensus of the entire network. This is why blockchain is considered trustworthy—it removes the need for a central authority and makes tampering practically impossible.
